_why: Recorded runtimes for EVERY CI job (okengine#898).
A timeout is a CLAIM about what a job costs. Until okengine#898 this file only had to evidence
jobs claiming a timeout below the shared-preamble floor, so a job ABOVE the floor never had to
prove its budget: full-suite held 30m while measuring 1,619-1,800s (a headroom factor of ~1.0)
and timed out green changes four times on 2026-09-26. Before that, diff-check and
mutation-targets carried 5m while needing 208-311s (!1018, !1020, !1013).
tests/test_ci_config.py asserts, for every job in the CI pipeline definition:
1. it has a timeout, own or inherited through `extends` (the project default lives outside
this repo, so a job without one has a budget no test can see);
2. it HAS an entry here with a real CI job id -- a job cannot escape by not being listed;
3. its timeout is at least headroom_factor x measured_s.
A job that has never run in CI cannot be measured; it may sit in `unmeasured` with a reason,
which the same test requires and reports, instead of a fabricated number.
measured_s is wall-clock (the CI job `duration`, queue time excluded) from real CI jobs, not a
local run and not an estimate. Unless a note says otherwise it is the SLOWEST successful run of
the job over the stated window, and job_id is that run. For parallel jobs it is the slowest
shard. Re-measure when a job's work changes; a stale number that is too LOW is the dangerous
direction, because it makes a tight budget look safe.

_why: Deadlines enforced INSIDE a job by a Makefile `timeout` wrapper, which a job's own `timeout:`
does not see. test-security shared TEST_FAST_DEADLINE=120 while its suite measured up to 95.5s
-- about 1.26x headroom -- and was killed at 89% complete on a contended runner (pipeline 9740,
job 110495). The `jobs` rule above could not catch it: that job's timeout was a comfortable
10m; the cap that fired was this inner one. Same contract as `jobs`: measured_s is a real CI
measurement with its job id, and the deadline must be at least headroom_factor x measured_s.
